theory.title: Describing personality with nuance
theory.explanation: At B2 level, avoid treating personality as a set of fixed labels. Describe observable behaviour, qualify your judgement and allow for context. Use modifiers to show degree, and hedging expressions when evidence is limited.

patterns.label: Tendencies
patterns.pattern: tend to + infinitive / have a tendency to + infinitive
examples: He tends to observe before speaking.
She has a tendency to take criticism personally.

patterns.label: Impressions
patterns.pattern: seem / appear + adjective; come across as + adjective or noun
examples: She came across as rather self-assured.

patterns.label: Typical reactions
examples: They are prone to making quick judgements.

patterns.label: Hedging
patterns.pattern: I wouldn't necessarily say that... / To some extent... / As far as I'm concerned...
examples: I wouldn't necessarily say he is unfriendly.
To some extent, first impressions are useful.

theory.tip: Describe what someone does before deciding what they are like. Use fairly, rather, somewhat, highly, remarkably or genuinely to make your meaning more precise.

content.passage: When Nina joined the research team, several colleagues assumed she was distant. During the first meetings, she rarely spoke unless someone asked her a direct question. She was also rather self-conscious about presenting ideas in front of experienced researchers. However, her manager, Daniel, encouraged everyone to keep an open mind. Over the following weeks, Nina gradually began to open up. Her comments were thoughtful, and she often noticed practical problems that other people had overlooked. She was particularly considerate when junior colleagues made mistakes: instead of criticising them in public, she offered useful suggestions afterwards. Nina was not especially outspoken, but she was self-assured when she had evidence to support an argument. On one occasion, she stood up for a colleague whose proposal had been dismissed too quickly. She explained the data calmly and persuaded the team to reconsider it. By the end of the project, the team's first impression had changed. Nina had not become a different person; people had simply learned to understand her behaviour more accurately. The experience reminded Daniel that personality is complex. Someone who appears reserved may be observant, and a confident speaker is not necessarily a good listener. First impressions can be useful, but they should remain provisional.

items.prompt: Describe a person who is approachable and considerate.
items.modelAnswer: Someone I admire is approachable because they make people feel at ease. They are also considerate and notice when others need support.

items.prompt: Explain why first impressions can be misleading.
items.modelAnswer: First impressions are based on limited information. Someone who seems reserved may simply need time to feel comfortable.

items.prompt: Describe a time when you misunderstood someone's behaviour.
items.modelAnswer: I once thought a colleague was uninterested because they were quiet. Later, I realised they were carefully listening before contributing.

items.prompt: Compare an outspoken person with a reserved person.
items.modelAnswer: An outspoken person tends to express ideas immediately, whereas a reserved person may prefer to think before speaking.

items.prompt: What qualities make someone reliable in a team?
items.modelAnswer: A reliable teammate keeps promises, communicates clearly and takes responsibility when something goes wrong.

items.prompt: How should people respond to criticism?
items.modelAnswer: They should try not to take it personally. It is useful to consider whether feedback is fair and specific.

items.prompt: Describe someone who has shown resilience.
items.modelAnswer: A friend showed resilience after a professional setback. They reflected on the experience and gradually rebuilt their confidence.

items.prompt: Can confidence become a disadvantage? Explain.
items.modelAnswer: Yes. If confidence turns into overconfidence, people may stop listening to others or considering alternative views.

items.prompt: How can we avoid judging people too quickly?
items.modelAnswer: We can ask questions, observe behaviour over time and give people the benefit of the doubt.

items.prompt: Give a short presentation on personality and communication.
items.modelAnswer: Personality can influence communication, but it does not determine every interaction. Context, confidence and experience also matter.

content.audioTranscript: Emma: What did you think of Daniel when you first met him? James: To be honest, I thought he was rather reserved. He didn't say very much, and I wasn't sure whether he was interested in the conversation. Emma: Really? I found him quite approachable. He seemed genuinely considerate, although he didn't come across as very self-assured at first. James: I suppose first impressions can be misleading. Once he started talking, he turned out to be remarkably thoughtful. He also had some interesting ideas. Emma: Exactly. I think he simply takes time to open up. He seems to have a tendency to observe people before expressing his opinions. James: That makes sense. I'd say he's reliable and open-minded. He also knows how to stand up for his colleagues without being too outspoken. Emma: I agree. It just shows that we shouldn't judge people too quickly.
